chunks: Inductor schematic symbol. The question: Draw the symbol for an inductor.
An inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in current, and its symbol is a coil too: a wire comes in, goes through three or four humps or loops, and goes out.
You label it with a reference designator such as L1 and its value in henries, like 10 microhenries.
Extra lines or dots added to the coil tell you about a core or about coupled windings.
The symbol is a cartoon of the part itself. An inductor really is a wire wound into turns, like a spring or an old phone cord seen from the side.
Each hump stands for one or more turns. Two parallel lines next to the coil stand for a core inside it, such as iron or ferrite.
The drawing does not show how many turns there are, so the label carries the value.
The schematic symbol is a cartoon of a real coil. Every hump is a turn, and every turn links the flux made by all the turns, which is why inductance scales as N².
Henry (H): the unit of inductance. Real parts are nH to mH. Core: the magnetic material the coil is wound around. Two lines in the symbol show it.
Saturation current: the current at which a cored inductor stops working properly. It matters as much as the inductance in power circuits.
Coupled inductors: two coils sharing a core, drawn with dots to show matching ends. This is a transformer.
Ferrite bead: a related part, often given its own rectangle symbol, that turns high-frequency noise into heat.
Draw a short wire, four humps in a row, and another short wire. Write L1 above it and 10 microhenries, 3 amps below it. That is a complete inductor on a schematic.
Add two straight lines alongside the humps and it becomes a cored inductor. Add an arrow through it and it is variable. That is the whole idea.
"An inductor is drawn as a coil: a lead, three or four humps, and another lead, labelled L1 with a value in henries, like 10 microhenries.
Two parallel lines next to the coil mean it has a magnetic core, an arrow through it means it's adjustable, and two coils with dots are coupled windings or a transformer.
A ferrite bead usually gets its own rectangle symbol because it acts more like a frequency-dependent resistor. For power parts I'd also annotate saturation current."
